walkthroughs.body_html:
Philosophy of Religion: Religious Experience, Problem of Evil — a core area of A-Level Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Philosophy of Religion: Religious Experience, Problem of Evil brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Philosophy of Religion: Religious Experience, Problem of Evil.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What are James's four marks of mystical experience?
options: Ineffability, noetic quality, transiency and passivity
Light, heat, sound and motion
Prayer, fasting, charity and pilgrimage
Fear, trembling, silence and song

mcqs.q: Which is an example of a corporate religious experience?
options: The Toronto Blessing
Paul's Damascus road conversion
Teresa of Avila's private visions
Augustine's conversion in the garden
The claim that omnipotence, perfect goodness and the existence of evil cannot all be true
Three proofs of God's existence
The three persons of the Trinity
Three types of religious experience

mcqs.q: What does Hick mean by calling the world a 'vale of soul-making'?
options: A challenging environment enables free moral and spiritual growth towards God
The world is a perfect paradise
Souls are manufactured in heaven
Evil is an illusion to be seen through

mcqs.q: Does explaining an experience's brain mechanism automatically debunk it?
options: Not by itself - how an experience is produced and whether its object is real are distinct questions, though naturalistic explanations can weaken its evidential force.
Any experience with a physiological trigger is thereby proved delusional.
The free will defence says humans choose for volcanoes to erupt.
Neuroscience has shown that experiences cannot occur in the brain.

mcqs.q: Does the free will defence cover earthquakes and disease?
options: Privation is the name of a demon in Augustine's writings.
Free will on its own neatly explains all natural disasters.
Its direct force concerns moral evil; natural evil requires extra resources, such as Augustine's account of a fallen world or Hick's claim that a law-governed, risky world is needed for soul-making.
The free will defence says humans choose for volcanoes to erupt.

mcqs.q: Is Augustine's 'privation' claim a denial that suffering is real?
options: Privation is the name of a demon in Augustine's writings.
Augustine said evil is an illusion nobody actually experiences.
Neuroscience has shown that experiences cannot occur in the brain.
No - privation means evil is an absence or corruption of good, like blindness as absence of sight; the suffering is real but evil is not a created substance.
